Gold medals inspire, sure, but real cultural impact comes when that energy fuels policy, funding, and access for those left off the field. National pride built on curated victories risks becoming performative theater unless it sparks tangible change—like community centers, scholarships, or equitable youth programs. True legacy isn’t measured in trophies, but in how many new dreams are made possible because someone dared to win—and then built a ladder behind them. We shouldn’t expect athletes to fix broken systems; instead, we should demand institutions create conditions where every kid can even dream of standing on that podium. Celebrating triumphs without addressing structural barriers just reinforces who “belongs” in the story—and who doesn’t. Let’s stop mistaking hype for healing and start measuring victory by how wide the circle of inclusion grows afterward.
conversation.subtopic: The cultural significance of athletic achievement and its impact on national identity.

conversation.content: Actually, I think we’re putting too much pressure on athletes to fix systemic issues—like expecting a gold medal to magically rewrite policy or fund schools. That’s not their job, and framing it that way lets institutions off the hook while turning champions into symbolic saviors instead of people who just excelled at their craft. Real change doesn’t come from podiums; it comes from voters, organizers, and policymakers who actually control budgets and laws. Let’s stop romanticizing sports as a cure-all and start demanding accountability from the systems that decide who gets access to fields, gear, and coaches in the first place. If we want inclusion, it has to be built into the structure—not tacked on after the victory lap.
conversation.subtopic: Generational support patterns within families and how they shape social responsibility.

conversation.content: In my family, my grandma paid for my cousin’s college tuition while working two jobs—she didn’t have a degree herself, but she believed education was the ladder out. Meanwhile, my uncle quietly covered rent for my sister when she lost her job, even though he was barely making ends meet. That kind of generational support isn’t just about money—it’s about modeling responsibility by putting others’ stability before your own comfort. I’ve seen cousins skip vacations to fund their kids’ coding camps, and grandparents trade in their cars to help with down payments. It’s not always loud or celebrated, but it’s how social responsibility gets passed down—not through speeches, but through silent sacrifices that say, “Your future matters more than my convenience.”
conversation.subtopic: Generational support patterns within families and how they shape social responsibility.

conversation.content: I completely agree—generational support within families is often quiet, unglamorous, and deeply rooted in sacrifice, not grand gestures. It’s the grandma working double shifts to pay tuition, the uncle covering rent without being asked, the grandparents trading their car for a down payment—it’s all about putting someone else’s stability ahead of your own comfort. This kind of responsibility isn’t taught through lectures; it’s modeled in everyday choices that say, “Your future matters more than my ease.” And while society celebrates big wins or policy changes, real social responsibility often starts at home, passed down through actions, not words. These small, consistent acts build resilience across generations, creating a foundation others can stand on—even if no one ever applauds them. That’s the true legacy: not trophies or headlines, but the unseen scaffolding that lets the next person rise. And honestly, if we want to talk about systemic change, maybe we should start by honoring the invisible architects—the families quietly building ladders for each other, one sacrifice at a time.

How do we measure the impact of those quiet, unseen sacrifices within families—do we even have metrics for love that shows up as rent payments or tuition checks?  
What happens when generational support gets stretched too thin, like a grandparent working two jobs while their own health declines?  
Is social responsibility truly passed down through actions alone, or does it require conversations about why those sacrifices matter in the first place?  
And if systemic inequality keeps forcing families to fill gaps that institutions should cover, are we romanticizing resilience instead of demanding change?  
Who decides what “support” looks like across different cultures—or is it always assumed to be financial, when emotional or logistical help might be just as vital?  
Why do we celebrate athletes’ triumphs but rarely spotlight the relatives who made those wins possible by going without?  
Could policy ever replicate the depth of care that flows naturally in families—or does that kind of responsibility only thrive outside bureaucracy?  
And if we’re serious about building equitable futures, shouldn’t we start by valuing and protecting the invisible labor that already holds so many communities together?

conversation.content: Actually, I think we’re romanticizing generational sacrifice as the backbone of social responsibility when it’s often a Band-Aid over systemic failure—families shouldn’t have to trade their health or retirement for their kids’ futures. If grandma’s working two jobs to pay tuition, that’s not resilience; that’s a broken system forcing love into the role of public policy. Real social responsibility means building structures that don’t require quiet suffering to function—because no amount of familial love should replace affordable education, healthcare, or housing. And while we honor those sacrifices, let’s also ask why they’re necessary in the first place—and who benefits from pretending families can fix what institutions refuse to. True legacy isn’t just passed down through silent acts—it’s built when society stops expecting them to carry the load alone.

Think of Kobe mentoring young Lakers not because he had to, but because he knew greatness multiplies when it’s shared. Or LeBron building schools in Akron so kids from his block could train like pros before they even hit high school—that’s not altruism, that’s redefining what success looks like. Too many careers are measured by personal stats or trophies, while the quiet enablers—the role players, the mentors, the coaches who stayed late—are erased from the narrative. Real legacy doesn’t hoard glory; it creates ecosystems where others can thrive alongside you. If your name stays in the story only because you demanded the spotlight, you’ve already lost. conversation.content: One concrete example is the Edge in NYC—built with reclaimed wood, solar panels, and a green roof that doubles as public space, proving sustainability can be both functional and iconic. Another is Singapore’s Gardens by the Bay, where biophilic design merges architecture with living ecosystems, reducing energy use while becoming a global landmark. Then there’s the Bullitt Center in Seattle, often called the “greenest commercial building in the world,” featuring composting toilets, rainwater harvesting, and net-zero energy—all without sacrificing aesthetics. Even historic renovations like London’s Tate Modern now integrate passive cooling and recycled materials, showing stewardship isn’t just for new builds. These aren’t niche experiments—they’re setting the standard for what modern architecture must become.

conversation.content:
The Federal Coffee Palace was a grand, French Second Empire style 560-room temperance hotel in Melbourne, built between 1886 and 1888 during the city's land boom, and demolished in 1972-73. It was located on Collins Street, near Spencer Street Station (now 555 Collins Street). The hotel is fondly remembered as one of the significant losses in Melbourne's architectural history.

As the largest and grandest product of the temperance movement in the southern hemisphere, "The Age" praised the £150,000 hotel as one of "Australia's most splendid" buildings and one of the world's most opulent hotels. It boasted seven main floors and two more in the corner tower, reaching 48m to the roof and  to the top of the dome, making it briefly the tallest building in Melbourne and Australia until the Australian Building's completion in 1890.

I had no idea Melbourne had such an extravagant hotel back then, especially one tied to the temperance movement. It's kind of wild to think something that grand was just demolished—imagine if it was still around today.

content.text: The 100 million square feet increase in resi- dential capacity we calculated was the net  result of upzonings and down zoning s in dif- ferent types of neighborhoods and involving  different types of zoning districts. In areas  that were rezoned from various non-resi- dential districts to residential-only districts,  we identified an increase in capacity of  about 40 million square feet. This increase  was offset, however, by an approximately 40  million square feet  decrease  in traditionally  residential areas (areas that were already  zoned for residential only uses in 2003).  The 100 million square feet net gain, then,  was effectively concentrated in areas that  were rezoned from a commercial or manu- facturing district to a mixed-use district.  While permitting residential development  in mixed-use areas is consistent with many  planning principles and may be an attractive  way for New York City to grow, not all zon- ing capacity in mixed use areas will be used  for residential development. To the extent  that City policymakers are depending on  mixed-used districts to accommodate resi- dential growth, it is important to recognize  that the amount of residential space that  actually will be built in those districts will  depend in part upon how the different uses  will compete for finite land area.

Our research looks at the impact of 76 rezon- ings that took place between 2003 and 2007,  the most recent year for which we had data  when we began this research. We focus only  on lots that already were, or would be (by  2007), zoned to permit residential use. To  provide a sense of the scale of the rezoning  activity: of the 816,000 lots that existed in  2003, approximately 188,000 were subject to  a City-initiated rezoning action by the end of  2007.  Figure A reveals how these rezonings  were distrib­ uted throughout the City.

Even though most downzoned lots were  located near transit stations, the overall  impact of the rezonings we studied appears  consistent with the City’s stated goal,  because the upzonings near transit added  much more capacity than the down zoning s  near rail stations took away. Specifically,  upzoned lots near transit gained about 181  million square feet of residential capacity  and downzoned lots near transit lost only  about 89 million square feet of capacity. As  a result, rezoned lots near transit accounted  for a vast majority of the citywide net  increase in capacity. Furthermore, of the  capacity added to upzoned lots further away  from rail stations, a large portion was in  the proposed Hudson Yards project area in  Manhattan, where an extension of the 7 line  subway is currently underway. If we exclude  the Hudson Yards rezoning, the rezonings  we studied actually resulted in a small net  decrease in residential development capac- ity in areas further away from rail stations,  consistent with the City’s goals.

content.text: sites in 2007, we see only a 25 million square  feet increase in residential development  capacity. Some soft sites disappeared dur- ing this period because they were the loca- tion of new development. More significantly  though, a lot of the capacity being added  through upzonings was not enough to make  the affected lots soft. In other words, even  after being upzoned, some of these lots were  still already developed at close to their full  capacity, so were unlikely to be redeveloped  with new housing in the near future. At the  same time, by removing development capac- ity, the City’s down zoning s made many  other lots that had been soft in 2003 more  or less fully developed as of 2007.

We estimate changes in residential develop- ment capacity at the lot level. Accordingly,  all estimates of capacity changes for the City,  community districts, boroughs and other  geographic areas, including area within and  beyond a half mile walking distance from rail  transit, are aggregations of lot-level data.

Our analysis classifies as “contextual-only”  any zoning change to a lot that does not  increase or decrease its residential devel- opment capacity by more than  $10\%$  . Most  of the lots rezoned between 2003 and  2007 fall into this category (particularly in  Staten Island and Queens).

- **Formwork**: Surrounds the concrete wall, consisting of vertical and horizontal timber boards (boarding) held in place by various structural elements.
- **M.S. Bars**: Positioned horizontally across the formwork, labeled near the top, used for reinforcement.
- **Wedges**: Shown at multiple points, these are triangular blocks inserted between the formwork and other structural elements to tighten and secure the assembly.
- **Timber Spacer**: Placed horizontally between the formwork and the bracing system, ensuring correct spacing.
- **Bolt with Nut & Head**: Runs horizontally through the formwork, securing the assembly together.

conversation.content:
How do we measure the success of sustainable architecture—by energy savings alone, or by how it reshapes community well-being and urban ecosystems?  
And if green buildings are becoming the norm, why aren’t more cities mandating biophilic design or circular material use in public projects?
conversation.subtopic: How environmental stewardship is becoming a core value in modern architecture.

conversation.content:
How do we ensure sustainable architecture doesn’t just check eco-boxes but actually transforms how people live, work, and connect with nature?  
And if green roofs and solar panels are now standard, why are so many new developments still ignoring urban heat islands or biodiversity loss?  
Who’s holding developers accountable when “sustainable” becomes a marketing buzzword instead of a lived reality?  
Can a building truly be stewarded by its community—or is that just another layer of performative responsibility?
conversation.subtopic: How environmental stewardship is becoming a core value in modern architecture.

conversation.content: Actually, calling environmental stewardship a “core value” in modern architecture feels more like branding than reality—because if it were truly foundational, we wouldn’t still see developers slap solar panels on glass towers while ignoring urban heat islands or displacing communities. Sure, the Bullitt Center and Gardens by the Bay are stunning, but they’re outliers, not the norm—and that’s the problem. When “sustainability” becomes a checkbox for LEED certification or a marketing hook for luxury condos, it’s not stewardship—it’s greenwashing. Real environmental responsibility means prioritizing local ecosystems over Instagrammable green roofs, and designing for resilience, not just efficiency. And let’s be honest: until cities mandate circular materials, passive cooling, and community-driven planning—not just incentivize them—this whole “core value” narrative is performative. Stewardship isn’t about making buildings look eco-friendly; it’s about ensuring they don’t harm the people or planet around them. If architects are serious, they’ll stop designing for awards and start designing for survival.
conversation.subtopic: How environmental stewardship is becoming a core value in modern architecture.

conversation.content: You’re right—calling it a “core value” feels performative when most developments still prioritize aesthetics over actual ecological impact. Real stewardship means designing for resilience, not just efficiency: think passive cooling in heat-vulnerable neighborhoods, or community gardens replacing luxury rooftop pools. The Bullitt Center isn’t the future—it’s the exception, and until cities mandate circular materials and equitable access to green space, we’re just rearranging deck chairs on a sinking ship. Stewardship shouldn’t be a buzzword; it should be the baseline, baked into every zoning law and building code.
conversation.subtopic: How environmental stewardship is becoming a core value in modern architecture.

conversation.content: Absolutely—environmental stewardship isn’t just a trend in architecture, it’s becoming the non-negotiable foundation. When buildings like the Bullitt Center or Gardens by the Bay prove that sustainability and beauty can coexist, they set a new standard—not an exception. The real test is whether cities and developers stop treating green design as a marketing add-on and start embedding it into every project, from zoning laws to material choices.
conversation.subtopic: How environmental stewardship is becoming a core value in modern architecture.

conversation.content: Environmental stewardship in architecture isn’t just about slapping solar panels on a skyscraper—it’s about rethinking how buildings breathe with their surroundings, from passive cooling in vulnerable neighborhoods to using materials that don’t poison the planet. The Bullitt Center and Gardens by the Bay aren’t outliers; they’re blueprints for what every city should demand, not reward as exceptions. If we’re serious about sustainability, we need policies that force developers to prioritize ecosystems over aesthetics, and communities over Instagrammable green roofs. Real stewardship means designing not for awards, but for survival—where every structure serves people, place, and planet, not just profit.
conversation.subtopic: How environmental stewardship is becoming a core value in modern architecture.

conversation.content: I’m skeptical that environmental stewardship is truly a core value in modern architecture—it still feels more like a marketing tactic than a foundational principle. Sure, we celebrate the Bullitt Center or Gardens by the Bay, but how many new developments actually prioritize local ecosystems over luxury amenities or LEED points? Until cities mandate circular materials and equitable green access—not just incentivize them—this “core value” narrative rings hollow. content.text: Adding textual context To examine whether web text is useful for answering commonsense questions, we add textual information to each question in the following way: We issue a web query to Google search for every question and candidate answer, concatenating the answer to the question, e.g.,  ‘What does a parent tell their child to do after they’ve played with a lot of toys?   $^+$  “clean room”’ . We take the ﬁrst 100 result snip- pets for each of the ﬁve answer candidates, yield- ing a context of 500 snippets per question. Using this context, we can investigate the performance of reading comprehension (RC) models on C OM - MONSENSE QA.

content.text: When answering a question, people often draw upon their rich world knowledge in addi- tion to the particular context. Recent work has focused primarily on answering questions given some relevant document or context, and required very little general background. To investigate question answering with prior knowledge, we present C OMMONSENSE QA: a challenging new dataset for commonsense question answering. To capture common sense beyond associations, we extract from C ON - CEPT N ET  ( Speer et al. ,  2017 ) multiple target concepts that have the same semantic relation to a single source concept. Crowd-workers are asked to author multiple-choice questions that mention the source concept and discrim- inate in turn between each of the target con- cepts. This encourages workers to create ques- tions with complex semantics that often re- quire prior knowledge. We create 12,247 ques- tions through this procedure and demonstrate the difﬁculty of our task with a large number of strong baselines. Our best baseline is based on BERT-large ( Devlin et al. ,  2018 ) and ob- tains   $56\%$   accuracy, well below human perfor- mance, which is  $89\%$  .

AMT workers saw, for every question set, the question concept and three answer concepts. They were asked to formulate three questions, where all questions contain the question concept. Then, for each question, workers choose an additional distractor from C ONCEPT N ET  (in italics), and author one themselves (in bold).

For each question, we explicitly annotated the types of commonsense skills that a human uses to answer the question. We allow multiple com- monsense skills per questions, with an average of 1.75 skills per question. Figure  3  provides three example annotations. Each annotation contains a node for the answer concept, and other nodes for concepts that appear in the question or latent con- cepts. Labeled edges describe the commonsense skill that relates the two nodes. We deﬁned com- monsense skills based on the analysis of  LoBue and Yates  ( 2011 ), with slight modiﬁcations to ac- commodate the phenomena in our data. Table  3 presents the skill categories we used, their deﬁni- tion and their frequency in the analyzed examples.

1. We ﬁlter triplets with general relations (e.g., RelatedTo ) or relations that are already well-explored in NLP (e.g.,  IsA ). In total we use 22 relations. 2. We ﬁlter triplets where one of the concepts is more than four words or not in English. 3. We ﬁlter triplets where the edit distance be- tween    $c_{1}$   and    $c_{2}$   is too low. This results in a set of 236,208 triplets    $(q,r,a)$  , where we call the ﬁrst concept the  question con- cept  and the second concept the  answer concept . We aim to generate questions that contain the question concept and where the answer is the an- swer concept. To create multiple-choice questions we need to choose  distractors  for each question. Sampling distractors at random from C ONCEPT - N ET  is a bad solution, as such distractors are easy to eliminate using simple surface clues.

content.text: b LM1B  Inspired by  Trinh and Le  ( 2018 ), we employ a large language model (LM) from  Joze- fowicz et al.  ( 2016 ), which was pre-trained on the One Billion Words Benchmark ( Chelba et al. , 2013 ). We use this model in two variations. In the ﬁrst (LM1B- CONCAT ), we simply concate- nate each answer to the question. In the second (LM1B- REP ), we ﬁrst cluster questions according to their ﬁrst two words. Then, we recognize ﬁve high-frequency preﬁxes that cover   $35\%$   of the de- velopment set (e.g.,  “what is” ). We rephrase ques- tions that ﬁt into one of these preﬁxes as a declar- ative sentence that contains the answer. E.g., we rephrase  “What is usually next to a door?”  and the candidate answer  “wall”  to  “Wall is usually next to a door” . For questions that do not start with the above preﬁxes, we concatenate the answer as in LM1B- CONCAT . In both variations we return the answer with highest LM probability.

We analyzed the distribution of ﬁrst and second words in the formulated questions along with ex- ample questions. Figure  4  presents the breakdown. Interestingly, only  $44\%$   of the ﬁrst words are WH- words. In about  $5\%$   of the questions, formulators used ﬁrst names to create a context story, and in  $7\%$   they used the word    $"i f"$   to present a hypothet- ical question. This suggests high variability in the question language.

content.text: The prior evaluations reveal the relative perfor- mance differences between approaches. Here, we identify trends per and between approaches. We sample 50 informal sentences total from both do- mains and then analyze the outputs from each model. We present sample sentences in Table  7 .

Formality: Following PT16, workers rate the formality of the source style sentence, the target style reference rewrite and the target style model outputs on a discrete scale of -3 to   $^{+3}$  described as:  -3: Very Informal, -2: Informal, -1: Somewhat Informal, 0: Neutral, 1: Somewhat Formal, 2: Formal and 3: Very Formal .

Since we want our tune and test sets to be of higher quality compared to the train set, we re- cruit a set of 85 expert workers for this anno- tation who had a   $100\%$   acceptance rate for our task and who had previously done more than 100 rewrites. Further, we collect multiple references for the tune/test set to adapt PBMT tuning and evaluation techniques to our task. We collect four different rewrites per sentence using our expert workers by randomly assigning sentences to the experts until four rewrites for each sentence are obtained.   To create our tune and test sets for the informal  to  formal  direction, we sample an addi- tional 3,000 informal sentences for our tune set and 1,500 sentences for our test set from each of the two domains.

content.text: We perform human-based evaluation to assess model outputs on the four criteria: formality , ﬂuency ,  meaning  and  overall . For a subset of 500 sentences from the test sets of both  Entertainment & Music  and  Family & Relationship  domains, we collect ﬁve human judgments per sentence per criteria using Amazon Mechanical Turk as follows:

Quantitative Analysis: While rewriting sen- tences more formally, humans tend to make a wide range of lexical/character-level edits. In Figure  1 , we plot the distribution of the character-level Lev- enshtein edit distance between the original infor- mal and the formal rewrites in the train set and observe a standard deviation of    $\sigma=19.39$   with a mean  $\mu=28.85$  . Next, we look at the difference in the formality level of the original informal and the formal rewrites in GYAFC. We ﬁnd that the classiﬁer trained on the  Answers  genre of PT16 dataset correlates poorly (Spearman  $\rho\,{=}\,0.38)$  ) with human judgments when tested on our domain spe- ciﬁc datasets. Hence, we collect formality judg- ments on a scale of  $^{-3}$   to  $+1$  , similar to PT16, for an additional 5000 sentences each from both do- mains and obtain a formality classiﬁer with higher correlation (Spearman    $\rho=0.56)$  ). We use this re- trained classiﬁer for our evaluation in    $\S5$   as well.

The following quantitative and qualitative analy- ses are aimed at characterizing the changes be- tween the original informal sentence and its formal rewrite in the GYAFC train split.   We present our analysis here on only the E&M domain data since we observe similar patterns in F&R.

content.text: Qualitative Analysis: To understand what stylistic choices differentiate formal from infor- mal text, we perform an analysis similar to PT16 and look at 50 rewrites from both domains and record the frequency of the types of edits that workers made when creating a more formal sen- tence.   In contrast to PT16, we observe a higher percentage of phrasal paraphrases   $(47\%)$  , edits to punctuations   $(40\%)$   and expansion of contractions  $(12\%)$  . This is reﬂective of our sentences coming from very informal domains of Yahoo Answers. Similar to PT16, we also observe capitalization  $(46\%)$   and normalization   $(10\%)$  .

ﬁcacy of the metrics ( § 6.3 ) and present a manual analysis ( § 6.4 ). We randomly select 500 sentences from each test set and run all ﬁve models. We use the entire train and tune split for training and tun- ing. We discuss results only on the E&M domain and list results on the F&R domain in the supple- mentary material.

Yahoo Answers,   a question answering forum, contains a large number of informal sentences and allows redistribution of data. Hence, we use the Yahoo Answers L6 corpus 5   to create our GYAFC dataset of informal and formal sentence pairs. In order to ensure a uniform distribution of data, we remove sentences that are questions, contain URLs, and are shorter than 5 words or longer than 25. After these preprocessing steps,   $40~\mathrm{mil}.$  - lion sentences remain. The Yahoo Answers corpus consists of several different domains like  Business, Entertainment & Music, Travel, Food,  etc. PT16 show that the formality level varies signiﬁcantly across different genres. In order to control for this variation, we work with two speciﬁc domains that contain the most informal sentences and show results on training and testing within those cate- gories. We use the formality classiﬁer from PT16 to identify informal sentences. We train this clas- siﬁer on the  Answers  genre of the PT16 corpus which consists of nearly 5,000 randomly selected sentences from Yahoo Answers manually anno- tated on a scale of -3 (very informal) to 3 (very for- mal).   We ﬁnd that the domains of  Entertainment & Music  and  Family & Relationships  contain the most informal sentences and create our GYAFC dataset using these domains. Table  2  shows the number of formal and informal sentences in all of Yahoo Answers corpus and within the two selected domains. Sentences with a score less than 0 are considered as informal and sentences with a score greater than 0 are considered as formal.
